screens.title: Understanding High Availability Concepts in Junos
screens.narratorSegment: High availability is the practice of designing networks to keep services running even when components fail. In enterprise environments, even short outages can have large operational and financial consequences. In this lesson you will learn what HA means in a Junos-powered network, why separating the control plane from the data plane matters, and how features like Routing Engine redundancy and Graceful Routing Engine Switchover reduce downtime. We will ground these ideas with a concrete configuration and verification workflow you can apply in a lab. You will see how redundancy eliminates single points of failure, how synchronized state reduces reconvergence time, and what common misconfigurations to avoid. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain control-plane and data-plane roles, enable and verify GRES, and reason about fault tolerance and rapid recovery in a Junos deployment. Think about an outage you might face at work: after this lesson you will be able to explain which HA controls reduce its impact and why.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Understanding High Availability
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Understanding High Availability Concepts in Junos

Learn how Junos separates control and forwarding, how redundancy is built, and why Graceful Routing Engine Switchover matters for continuous service.

In this lesson
Core HA principles, RE redundancy, and GRES configuration.
Coming up
Verification commands and a hands-on scenario.
Why it matters
Reduce reconvergence time and avoid service interruption during RE failover.
Visual preview
Control Plane
Routing Engine state, protocols, adjacencies
Data Plane
PFEs handle high-speed packet forwarding
GRES
Synchronized RE state for smooth switchover

Use the hands-on activity later in the chapter to practice enabling and verifying GRES in a lab. This preview gives you the mental model needed to follow the configuration steps.

Quick topics
Separation of planes
Allows independent redundancy for control and forwarding.
RE redundancy
Primary and backup RE synchronize state for takeover.
GRES
Graceful switchover keeps routing state intact during failover.
Short orientation

Start by learning the conceptual separation, then practice enabling GRES, and finally verify synchronization and behavior in a safe lab. This order reduces risk in production deployments.

Each objective is practical: explaining HA helps you design networks that avoid single points of failure; distinguishing planes helps you choose the right redundancy for each function; describing Routing Engine behavior prepares you to test failure scenarios; and enabling GRES gives you a concrete operational mechanism for seamless control-plane transition. For example, after practicing the hands-on steps you will be able to enable GRES in a lab and interpret the output of verification commands to confirm synchronization. We will also emphasize common mistakes, such as assuming dual Routing Engines imply seamless state sync, so you can avoid those pitfalls. These skills matter because they reduce outage windows and improve service continuity for users and applications.

screens.title: What is High Availability (HA)?
screens.narratorSegment: High availability is a design approach that minimizes downtime and keeps services operational despite failures. At its heart, HA eliminates single points of failure by duplicating critical components and creating alternative paths. In networking this often means redundant hardware, duplicate links, and synchronized state so that a replacement component can take over without service interruption. An example is having two Routing Engines where one is primary and the other is standby. If the primary fails, the standby becomes active to preserve control-plane functions. The goals of HA are fault tolerance — the ability to continue operation when parts fail — and rapid recovery — restoring full functionality quickly after a fault. Common patterns include active/standby redundancy, active/active where supported, and path diversity for links. A frequent misconception is thinking redundancy alone guarantees zero downtime. Redundancy is necessary but not sufficient; synchronization and careful failover design matter. For instance, if you have a standby Routing Engine but it does not have synchronized kernel and routing state, a switchover still causes reconvergence and traffic loss. Always pair redundancy with state synchronization and verification checks so you achieve the practical goals of HA. How might you prioritize HA features for the most critical applications on your network?

keyIdea.text: Redundancy plus synchronized state and verification yields practical high availability; hardware copies alone do not eliminate downtime.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is High Availability?

Definition and goals

High availability minimizes downtime by removing single points of failure and enabling rapid recovery. It combines redundancy with state synchronization and verification.

Fault tolerance: continue operating when parts fail.
Rapid recovery: restore full functionality quickly.
Design patterns: active/standby, active/active, path diversity.
Concrete example
Two Routing Engines: primary handles routing protocols; backup stays hot and synchronizes state so it can take over without rebooting the control plane.
Key Takeaway

Redundancy must be paired with mechanisms that preserve and synchronize state to achieve true HA.

Misconceptions

  • - Having two of the same component does not guarantee non-disruptive failover unless state is synchronized.
  • - HA is more than hardware redundancy; you must plan for synchronization, testing, and verification.
Why this matters

Applications like voice, video, and critical databases are sensitive to even short reconvergence windows. Good HA reduces user impact and business risk.

screens.title: Control Plane vs Data Plane
screens.narratorSegment: Junos separates the control plane and the data plane so each can be made resilient in the way that best suits its function. The control plane is the brain: it runs routing protocols, maintains routing tables, and manages protocol adjacencies. This typically resides on the Routing Engine. The data plane is the highway: Packet Forwarding Engines or line cards forward packets at high speed using information derived from the control plane. Why does this separation matter for HA? Because each plane has different failure modes and recovery strategies. For the data plane, you often rely on hardware redundancy, multiple forwarding engines, and nonstop forwarding features that keep packets moving even if the control plane briefly resets. For the control plane, you rely on redundant Routing Engines and synchronization features like GRES so routing state survives a switchover. A common misconception is expecting control-plane redundancy to automatically protect forwarding during complex failures. In practice you design independent redundancy for each plane and test both. For example, a control-plane switchover with GRES minimizes protocol reconvergence, while good data-plane design keeps forwarding steady even if control-plane processes restart. Reflect: which plane's availability would you prioritize for low-latency applications and why?

keyIdea.title: Separate strategies
keyIdea.text: Control plane and data plane require different HA strategies; design redundancy and synchronization appropriate to each plane's role.

content.html:
Comparison › Control Plane vs Data Plane

Control Plane (Routing Engine)

Runs routing protocols, builds routing tables, and manages adjacencies. Critical for network decision-making but not optimized for bulk forwarding.

Role: protocol management and topology convergence
Redundancy: dual Routing Engines with hot-standby and GRES for synchronized state
Example
When a link flaps, the control plane updates routing tables and informs the data plane which next-hops to use.

Data Plane (PFEs / Line Cards)

Handles high-speed packet forwarding using rules from the control plane. Designed for performance and continuity.

Role: packet forwarding at line rate
Redundancy: multiple PFEs, nonstop forwarding mechanisms maintain forwarding while control plane updates
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Treat planes separately: redundancy and recovery expectations differ and must be designed and tested independently.

screens.title: Routing Engine Redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: High-end Juniper devices commonly support dual Routing Engines: one primary that performs control-plane duties and a backup that remains in hot standby. The backup continuously synchronizes critical state with the primary so it can take over quickly if the primary fails. Synchronization includes configuration, kernel state, and often fabric data needed for seamless transition. The master/backup relationship includes role election and priorities; operational commands show which RE is master and which is backup. In practice, you plan redundancy so the backup is always updated and reachable. A key operational habit is to verify synchronization status after configuration. If synchronization is incomplete you risk the backup performing a cold start after a failure, causing routing adjacencies to rebuild and traffic to be disrupted. Another misconception is thinking the backup consumes no resources — hot standby requires careful resource and state management and increases overall system complexity. A practical example: in a dual-RE chassis, a fiber interface flap should not require a full control-plane rebuild if the backup has synchronized kernel and routing information. The architecture design goal is to make the switchover near-invisible to applications and users.

keyIdea.title: RE redundancy goal
keyIdea.text: Keep a backup Routing Engine synchronized with the primary so it can assume control quickly and avoid control-plane rebuilds.

content.html:
Architecture › Routing Engine Redundancy

Master and Backup RE

The primary RE handles routing and management. The backup RE stays hot and synchronizes state so it can become primary with minimal disruption.

Config sync: ensures identical configurations
Kernel sync: preserves forwarding decisions and table state
Fabric sync: aligns internal fabric and hardware state
Operational note

After enabling redundancy, confirm synchronization and test in a lab. Do not assume the backup will always have current state without verification.

Scenario
If the primary RE reboots during maintenance, a synchronized backup can take over immediately and keep forwarding intact if GRES is enabled and data-plane state is preserved.
Common mistake

Assuming dual REs alone mean automatic graceful recovery. You must enable features that synchronize state, then verify them.

screens.title: What is GRES?
screens.narratorSegment: Graceful Routing Engine Switchover is a Junos feature that lets a backup Routing Engine take over control-plane duties without disrupting forwarded traffic or forcing routing protocols to reconverge from scratch. When GRES is enabled, the backup maintains a synchronized copy of important state from the primary: interface states, next-hop information, routing protocol adjacency state, and kernel tables. During a switchover the backup promotes itself to primary and immediately resumes control-plane functions using that synchronized state. The result is a shorter or near-transparent transition compared to a cold switchover, which forces the new RE to rebuild state and causes significant packet loss. A concrete example: with GRES enabled, a planned RE reboot can be executed while the backup becomes primary with routing adjacencies still intact, preserving application-level sessions. A key misconception is believing GRES is automatic in dual-RE systems; it must be explicitly configured and verified. Another important point is that GRES depends on healthy synchronization mechanisms and a reliable path between REs. Without that, the backup cannot maintain the state needed for a graceful takeover. Consider whether your current RE pair has GRES enabled and how you would verify it in your environment.

keyIdea.title: GRES purpose
keyIdea.text: GRES preserves control-plane state on the backup RE so a switchover completes with minimal reconvergence and reduced traffic disruption.

content.html:
Definition › What is GRES?

GRES explained

GRES enables the backup Routing Engine to maintain a synchronized copy of the primary's state and take over without forcing routing protocols to rebuild adjacencies.

Synchronized items: interface states and next-hops
Protocol adjacencies and kernel state
Real example
Planned RE reboot with GRES: backup assumes primary role and routing state persists, reducing outage time significantly.
Verification focus
GRES must be enabled in configuration and synchronization must report Done for config, kernel, and fabric. If any show check reports incomplete, treat GRES as non-functional.
Common mistake

Assuming GRES is present simply because two REs exist. Enable it and verify its status before relying on it in production.

screens.title: How GRES Works Internally
screens.narratorSegment: GRES works by keeping an up-to-date copy of critical control-plane information on the backup Routing Engine and orchestrating a handover that preserves that state. The process begins with continuous synchronization: the primary RE pushes configuration changes, kernel state, and fabric information to the backup. This ensures both REs have matching views of interfaces, next-hops, and routing tables. When a switchover is triggered — whether due to failure or a planned switch — the backup promotes itself to master and activates the synchronized kernel and routing state. Since adjacencies and next-hop information are already present, routing protocols often continue without a full reconvergence. The steps you should remember are: enable GRES in configuration, confirm synchronization is Done for configuration, kernel, and fabric, and only then consider the switchover safe. A practical mistake is skipping verification and assuming synchronization; that leads to a cold restart and prolonged outage. Another nuance is the synchronization path: the physical and logical links between REs must be healthy for GRES to work. In summary, GRES reduces reconvergence by making the backup effectively pre-warmed with the control-plane state. What synchronization check would you prioritize before a maintenance window?

keyIdea.title: GRES sequence
keyIdea.text: Continuous synchronization followed by a coordinated promotion of the backup RE preserves kernel and routing state during switchover.

content.html:
Process Flow › How GRES Works Internally

Continuous synchronization

  1. Primary pushes configuration and kernel state to backup continuously.
  2. Backup maintains protocol adjacencies and table snapshots where possible.
  3. System reports synchronization status as Done when aligned.
These steps ensure the backup is pre-warmed and ready to assume control without rebuilding state from scratch.

Switchover sequence

  1. Trigger or detect RE failure.
  2. Backup promotes to master using synchronized state.
  3. Control-plane functions resume with minimal reconvergence.
Key Takeaway

GRES reduces the time to restore control-plane functionality by relying on an up-to-date backup that can take over immediately.

Pitfall: a broken synchronization path causes the backup to perform a cold start and forces full reconvergence.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Configure GRES — CLI Template

CLI steps

Follow these commands in a lab environment first. The template below is the chapter's canonical example.

# Step 1 & 2: Access CLI and enter configuration mode
# user@router> configure

# Step 3: Configure GRES on the chassis
set chassis redundancy graceful-switchover

# Step 4: Commit the changes
commit and-quit

# Step 5: Verify GRES status and RE roles
# user@router> show chassis redundancy
# user@router> show chassis routing-engine

# Step 6 (Optional): Initiate a manual RE switchover (DO NOT do this in production without careful planning!)
# user@router> request chassis routing-engine master switch
After committing, always run the verification commands and inspect the output fields for configuration and kernel synchronization and for the GRES enabled flag.
Safety note
A manual switchover should only be performed in a lab or scheduled maintenance window. Unplanned switchovers can interact with other systems and cause unexpected interruptions.
Pro Tip

Add verification commands to your runbook so you never skip the synchronization checks before a maintenance window.

screens.title: Verify GRES — Expected Output
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the most important step after configuration. The chapter includes the expected output for show chassis redundancy which lists the state for each Routing Engine slot and indicates whether synchronization tasks are Done and whether GRES is enabled. When you run show chassis redundancy you want to see configuration, kernel, and fabric synchronization reported as Done and GRES enabled as Yes for both slots. This output confirms a healthy synchronization path. A practical example: you should see Slot 0 as Master and Slot 1 as Backup with GRES enabled on both. If any synchronization field shows incomplete or an unexpected role, troubleshoot the synchronization path and configuration before relying on the backup for a switchover. A common operational check is to re-run these commands after a configuration change and before maintenance windows. If you detect any problem, resolve it and repeat verification. The quality of your HA depends on consistent verification habits and not only on initial configuration. Verification › Verify GRES — Expected Output

Expected command output

The chapter provides a canonical show chassis redundancy output. Look for the fields shown below when you verify your setup.
Routing Engine status:

screens.title: Mistakes, Pitfalls, and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Even experienced engineers can make avoidable mistakes when designing or enabling HA. One frequent pitfall is assuming that having dual Routing Engines guarantees a graceful switchover. Without explicitly enabling GRES and validating synchronization, a switchover behaves like a cold restart and forces routing protocols to reconverge — causing traffic disruption. Another error is neglecting the synchronization path: if the links or internal fabric used for synchronization are misconfigured or degraded, the backup cannot maintain the necessary state. Some teams also skip verification after configuration changes; synchronization can be broken by unrelated modifications or intermittent hardware issues. A final area to watch is testing: performing a manual switchover in production without coordination can expose hidden dependencies and cause outages. The avoidant strategy is clear: enable GRES, verify the show outputs, test in a lab environment, and add synchronization checks to any change-control runbook. A simple habit is to require a green verification checklist before scheduling maintenance. screens.title: Fault Tolerance and Rapid Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Fault tolerance and rapid recovery are the operational outcomes HA design strives to achieve. Fault tolerance means the network can continue to operate despite component failures; rapid recovery means the system restores full service quickly after a fault. In enterprise networks these outcomes translate directly to business continuity: uninterrupted access to critical applications, consistent voice and video quality, and reliable data flows. From a technical perspective, achieving these outcomes requires layered measures: redundant hardware, synchronized state for control-plane elements, path diversity for links, and automated verification and monitoring. For instance, enabling GRES addresses one part of the puzzle by preserving control-plane state across a Routing Engine switchover, but you must also ensure data-plane continuity through nonstop forwarding or redundant PFEs. A planning pitfall is optimizing only for one metric, such as hardware redundancy, without mechanisms to preserve state or test recovery. The right approach balances redundancy, synchronization, and verification practices so faults are tolerated and recovery is predictable. As you design HA, ask which failures cause the largest user impact and focus your efforts where they reduce that impact most effectively.

Concept › Fault Tolerance and Rapid Recovery

Fault tolerance

Design so the system continues to operate despite failures by removing single points of failure and adding redundancy.

Techniques include redundant Routing Engines, PFEs, multiple uplinks, and diversified paths so a single failure does not stop service.

Rapid recovery

Make restoration fast and predictable by using synchronization features like GRES and by automating verification and test procedures.

Key Takeaway

Prioritize HA investments where they reduce customer impact the most: combine redundancy with synchronization and verification for reliable recovery.

fullNarratorScript:
High availability is the practice of designing networks to keep services running even when components fail. In enterprise environments, even short outages can have large operational and financial consequences. In this lesson you will learn what HA means in a Junos-powered network, why separating the control plane from the data plane matters, and how features like Routing Engine redundancy and Graceful Routing Engine Switchover reduce downtime. We will ground these ideas with a concrete configuration and verification workflow you can apply in a lab. You will see how redundancy eliminates single points of failure, how synchronized state reduces reconvergence time, and what common misconfigurations to avoid. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain control-plane and data-plane roles, enable and verify GRES, and reason about fault tolerance and rapid recovery in a Junos deployment. Think about an outage you might face at work: after this lesson you will be able to explain which HA controls reduce its impact and why.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain core high availability principles, distinguish between the control plane and the data plane in Junos, describe how Routing Engine redundancy works, and configure and verify Graceful Routing Engine Switchover. Each objective is practical: explaining HA helps you design networks that avoid single points of failure; distinguishing planes helps you choose the right redundancy for each function; describing Routing Engine behavior prepares you to test failure scenarios; and enabling GRES gives you a concrete operational mechanism for seamless control-plane transition. For example, after practicing the hands-on steps you will be able to enable GRES in a lab and interpret the output of verification commands to confirm synchronization. We will also emphasize common mistakes, such as assuming dual Routing Engines imply seamless state sync, so you can avoid those pitfalls. These skills matter because they reduce outage windows and improve service continuity for users and applications.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying HA knowledge in a practical way. You will practice enabling GRES in configuration mode, committing the change, and interpreting verification command output to confirm synchronization. The hands-on steps are concrete: access the Junos CLI, set chassis redundancy graceful-switchover, commit, then run the show chassis redundancy and show chassis routing-engine commands to confirm kernel and configuration synchronization and that GRES is enabled. These steps are important because a misconfigured synchronization path can cause a switchover to act like a cold restart, forcing routing protocols to reconverge and causing traffic loss. In the lab we will also discuss safety: never perform a manual switchover in production without coordination. The objective is to produce repeatable verification habits you can use to sign off on HA readiness before maintenance windows or role changes.

High availability is a design approach that minimizes downtime and keeps services operational despite failures. At its heart, HA eliminates single points of failure by duplicating critical components and creating alternative paths. In networking this often means redundant hardware, duplicate links, and synchronized state so that a replacement component can take over without service interruption. An example is having two Routing Engines where one is primary and the other is standby. If the primary fails, the standby becomes active to preserve control-plane functions. The goals of HA are fault tolerance — the ability to continue operation when parts fail — and rapid recovery — restoring full functionality quickly after a fault. Common patterns include active/standby redundancy, active/active where supported, and path diversity for links. A frequent misconception is thinking redundancy alone guarantees zero downtime. Redundancy is necessary but not sufficient; synchronization and careful failover design matter. For instance, if you have a standby Routing Engine but it does not have synchronized kernel and routing state, a switchover still causes reconvergence and traffic loss. Always pair redundancy with state synchronization and verification checks so you achieve the practical goals of HA. How might you prioritize HA features for the most critical applications on your network?

Junos separates the control plane and the data plane so each can be made resilient in the way that best suits its function. The control plane is the brain: it runs routing protocols, maintains routing tables, and manages protocol adjacencies. This typically resides on the Routing Engine. The data plane is the highway: Packet Forwarding Engines or line cards forward packets at high speed using information derived from the control plane. Why does this separation matter for HA? Because each plane has different failure modes and recovery strategies. For the data plane, you often rely on hardware redundancy, multiple forwarding engines, and nonstop forwarding features that keep packets moving even if the control plane briefly resets. For the control plane, you rely on redundant Routing Engines and synchronization features like GRES so routing state survives a switchover. A common misconception is expecting control-plane redundancy to automatically protect forwarding during complex failures. In practice you design independent redundancy for each plane and test both. For example, a control-plane switchover with GRES minimizes protocol reconvergence, while good data-plane design keeps forwarding steady even if control-plane processes restart. Reflect: which plane's availability would you prioritize for low-latency applications and why?

High-end Juniper devices commonly support dual Routing Engines: one primary that performs control-plane duties and a backup that remains in hot standby. The backup continuously synchronizes critical state with the primary so it can take over quickly if the primary fails. Synchronization includes configuration, kernel state, and often fabric data needed for seamless transition. The master/backup relationship includes role election and priorities; operational commands show which RE is master and which is backup. In practice, you plan redundancy so the backup is always updated and reachable. A key operational habit is to verify synchronization status after configuration. If synchronization is incomplete you risk the backup performing a cold start after a failure, causing routing adjacencies to rebuild and traffic to be disrupted. Another misconception is thinking the backup consumes no resources — hot standby requires careful resource and state management and increases overall system complexity. A practical example: in a dual-RE chassis, a fiber interface flap should not require a full control-plane rebuild if the backup has synchronized kernel and routing information. The architecture design goal is to make the switchover near-invisible to applications and users.

Graceful Routing Engine Switchover is a Junos feature that lets a backup Routing Engine take over control-plane duties without disrupting forwarded traffic or forcing routing protocols to reconverge from scratch. When GRES is enabled, the backup maintains a synchronized copy of important state from the primary: interface states, next-hop information, routing protocol adjacency state, and kernel tables. During a switchover the backup promotes itself to primary and immediately resumes control-plane functions using that synchronized state. The result is a shorter or near-transparent transition compared to a cold switchover, which forces the new RE to rebuild state and causes significant packet loss. A concrete example: with GRES enabled, a planned RE reboot can be executed while the backup becomes primary with routing adjacencies still intact, preserving application-level sessions. A key misconception is believing GRES is automatic in dual-RE systems; it must be explicitly configured and verified. Another important point is that GRES depends on healthy synchronization mechanisms and a reliable path between REs. Without that, the backup cannot maintain the state needed for a graceful takeover. Consider whether your current RE pair has GRES enabled and how you would verify it in your environment.

GRES works by keeping an up-to-date copy of critical control-plane information on the backup Routing Engine and orchestrating a handover that preserves that state. The process begins with continuous synchronization: the primary RE pushes configuration changes, kernel state, and fabric information to the backup. This ensures both REs have matching views of interfaces, next-hops, and routing tables. When a switchover is triggered — whether due to failure or a planned switch — the backup promotes itself to master and activates the synchronized kernel and routing state. Since adjacencies and next-hop information are already present, routing protocols often continue without a full reconvergence. The steps you should remember are: enable GRES in configuration, confirm synchronization is Done for configuration, kernel, and fabric, and only then consider the switchover safe. A practical mistake is skipping verification and assuming synchronization; that leads to a cold restart and prolonged outage. Another nuance is the synchronization path: the physical and logical links between REs must be healthy for GRES to work. In summary, GRES reduces reconvergence by making the backup effectively pre-warmed with the control-plane state. What synchronization check would you prioritize before a maintenance window?
